name: Umananda Temple
significance: A brick Shiva shrine raised in 1694 on the Brahmaputra river island at Guwahati by order of the Ahom king Gadadhar Singha, standing on a site that also preserves traces of an earlier post-Gupta stone temple. Badly damaged in the 1897 Assam earthquake, it was rebuilt afterwards by a local merchant.
story: Shiva is said to have burnt Kamadeva to ashes here for disturbing his meditation, which is why the hillock is called Bhasmachala.

name: Navagraha Mandir
significance: An astronomy-linked shrine on Chitrachal Hill whose sanctum holds nine lingams for the nine celestial bodies, each draped in a colour assigned to its planet. Wrecked by the earthquake of 1697, it was rebuilt in full by the Ahom ruler Rajeswara Singha in 1752.

name: Basistha Temple
significance: An octagonal brick temple with a polygonal sikhara raised in 1764 under the Ahom king Rajeswar Singha on the remains of a stone temple of about the 11th century. It sits where three hill streams meet to form the Basistha and Bharalu rivers of Guwahati.
story: The site is held to be the ashrama of the sage Vasistha, and its sunken chamber is said to keep his footprint.

name: Hayagriva Madhava Temple
significance: A stone temple of 1583 on Manikut hill at Hajo, built by Raghudeva Narayan of the Koch dynasty, whose lowest wall course carries an unbroken frieze of elephants. Its outer walls are carved with the ten avatars of Vishnu and with scenes from the Ramayana and Mahabharata.

name: Sivadol
significance: A group of three temples to Shiva, Vishnu and Durga built in 1734 by Bar Raja Ambika, queen of the Ahom king Siva Singha, on the bank of the Sivasagar tank dug between 1731 and 1738. The main Sivadol rises about 104 feet under a gilded dome and is among the tallest temples in Assam.

name: Mahabhairav Temple
significance: A Shiva temple on a hillock in northern Tezpur, endowed during Ahom rule when Tungkhungia kings granted it land and appointed its priests and attendants. The old stone shrine has since been rebuilt in concrete, and the temple is now run by a committee under the Government of Assam.
story: The lingam is believed to be of living stone that slowly grows, and King Bana is said to have gained his prosperity by worshipping Shiva here.

name: Madan Kamdev
significance: A ruined temple complex of the Kamarupa Pala period, first noticed by Edward Dalton around 1855 and excavated from 1977, which uncovered a main temple and the remains of about a dozen more. Its sculpture, dated by the excavators to the 10th-12th centuries, includes Bhairava, Vishnu, Saraswati and celebrated Uma-Maheshwara couples.
story: Puranic tradition holds that Kamadeva, burnt to cinders by an angry Shiva, was reborn at this spot.

name: Sri Surya Pahar
significance: A hillside archaeological site near Goalpara where Hindu, Buddhist and Jain remains lie together, including hundreds of rock-cut Shiva lingas, about 25 rock-cut stupas of the early centuries CE and temple foundations excavated between 1992 and 2001. Some scholars have proposed it, rather than Guwahati, as the ancient capital Pragjyotishpura.
story: Local tradition says the sage Vyasa carved 99,999 lingas here in an attempt to raise a second Kashi.

name: Unakoti
significance: A Shaiva rock-cut site in northern Tripura carved with colossal reliefs, chief among them a Shiva head some thirty feet high with an elaborate headdress, along with a giant Ganesha and several Nandi figures. An inscription of the 11th-12th century records a pilgrim named Sri Jayadeva; the site is protected by the Archaeological Survey of India and was added to UNESCO's tentative list in December 2022.
story: Shiva is said to have travelled towards Kashi with one crore companions who overslept, and on waking alone he cursed them into stone, leaving one short of a crore.

name: Chaturdasha Temple
significance: Built in 1760 by King Krishna Manikya when the Tripura capital moved to Agartala, this temple enshrines the royal house's fourteen deities and is the focus of the Kharchi puja. Its dome copies the roof form of Tripuri village huts and is topped by a stupa-like finial suggesting Buddhist influence.

name: Rumtek Monastery
deity: Karma Kagyu lineage; seat of the Gyalwang Karmapa
significance: The Dharmachakra Centre, seat in exile of the Karmapa and principal monastery of the Karma Kagyu school, first built in the mid-18th century under the 12th Karmapa. The 16th Karmapa found it ruined after leaving Tibet in 1959 and had it rebuilt over four years, inaugurating it at Losar in 1966; it holds his relics in a golden stupa and houses the Karma Shri Nalanda Institute.

name: Pemayangtse Monastery
significance: One of Sikkim's oldest and most senior Nyingma monasteries, begun as a small lhakhang by Lama Lhatsun Chempo in 1647 and enlarged under the third Chogyal Chakdor Namgyal in 1705. Reserved for monks of pure lineage, its head lama held the privilege of anointing the Chogyals of Sikkim; the three-storey building has been repaired after the earthquakes of 1913 and 1960.

name: Tashiding Monastery
significance: A Nyingma monastery founded in West Sikkim in 1641 by Ngadak Sempa Chenpo Phunshok Rigzing and expanded in 1717 under the third Chogyal. Regarded as the spiritual centre of Sikkim, it keeps 41 chortens and stones carved with mantras.
story: A vase of holy water consecrated by Guru Padmasambhava is said to be kept here, and at the yearly Bhumchu festival the change in its water level is read as an omen for Sikkim's coming year.

name: Enchey Monastery
deity: Buddha and Padmasambhava; protectors Khangchendzonga and Yabdean
significance: A Nyingma monastery above Gangtok, first raised in the 1840s under the eighth Chogyal and rebuilt in its present form in 1909 during the regency of Sikyong Tulku. Gutted by fire in 1947 and restored the following year, it houses about ninety monks and remains under the authority of Pemayangtse.
story: The site is said to have been chosen by the tantric adept Lama Druptab Karpo, who flew here from Maenam Hill and set up a small gompa.

name: Parshuram Kund
deity: Parashurama, with a shrine to Devi Renuka
significance: A bathing pool on the Lohit river that is one of the best-known Hindu pilgrimage sites in Arunachal Pradesh, drawing large crowds at Makar Sankranti. The original kund was buried by the 1950 Assam earthquake, after which boulders settled into a ring in the riverbed and sadhus re-established the site in the 1970s.
story: Parashurama, his axe stuck fast to his hand after killing his mother Renuka, is said to have dipped his hands here, whereupon the axe fell away and his sin was washed off.

name: Malinithan
significance: A ruined temple site on the north bank of the Brahmaputra in Lower Siang district, where excavation exposed a carved stone plinth about eight feet high with sculptures of deities, animals and floral work. Masons' marks here match those at other Chutia-period sites such as the Tamreswari temple, and its absence from 10th-11th century texts places its construction later.
story: Sankardev's retelling has Krishna and Rukmini break their journey to Dwarka here, where Durga garlanded them with flowers, giving the place its name.

name: Shree Govindajee Temple
significance: The royal temple of Manipur adjoining the Imphal palace, commissioned by Maharaja Nara Singh in 1846 and rebuilt by Maharaja Chandrakriti after the earthquake of 1868, being reconsecrated in 1876. Its images were removed to Kongma during the Anglo-Manipur war of 1891 and reinstalled in 1908 beside the new palace.
story: Maharaja Jai Singh is said to have been told in a vision to carve Krishna's image from a jackfruit tree, work he began in 1776 and consecrated in 1779.

name: Sringeri Sharada Peetham
builtDisplay: 14th c. (Vijayanagara); tradition ascribes it to Adi Shankara
significance: One of the four cardinal mathas of the Advaita Vedanta tradition, on the bank of the Tunga, traditionally founded by Adi Shankara though its documented record begins in the 14th century. Vijayanagara rulers became its patrons after 1336 and financed the Vidyashankara temple completed in 1338, and its 12th acharya Vidyaranya advised the empire's founders; it has directed Smarta religious life across south India for six centuries.
story: Adi Shankara is said to have chosen the spot after seeing a cobra spread its hood to shade a pregnant frog from the sun.

name: Annapoorneshwari Temple
significance: A goddess temple at Horanadu in the Western Ghats of Chikkamagaluru district, on the bank of the Bhadra, known as Sri Kshetra Horanadu and celebrated for feeding every pilgrim who comes. It is a leading Devi shrine of Karnataka, though its founding date is not documented.
story: Its establishment is traditionally credited to the sage Agastya.

name: Kollur Mookambika Temple
style: Dravidian with Vijayanagara and Hoysala elements
significance: A major Shakta temple at the foot of the Kodachadri hills on the Souparnika river in Udupi district, dated to about 800 CE and associated with the patron Halugallu Veera Sangayya. Its sanctum holds a self-manifested linga together with a four-armed panchaloha image of the goddess, whose installation is ascribed to Adi Shankara.
story: The goddess is said to have struck the demon Mookasura dumb so that he could not ask Shiva for a boon, and then killed him when he harassed the sage Kola Maharshi.

name: Dharmasthala Temple
deity: Manjunatha (Shiva), with Ammanavaru and Jain guardian deities
significance: A temple of about 800 years' standing founded by the Jain chieftain Birmanna Pergade and his wife Ammu Ballalthi, and reconsecrated in the 16th century by the Madhva saint Vadiraja Tirtha. It is unusual in being administered for some twenty generations by a Jain Bunt family, the Heggades, while Madhva Brahmin priests conduct its worship.
story: Guardian spirits are said to have come to Birmanna Pergade seeking a home where dharma was kept, and told him to raise shrines for four protective deities.

name: Kukke Subramanya Temple
deity: Kartikeya as Subramanya, lord of serpents
significance: A serpent-worship centre on the Kumaradhara river in Dakshina Kannada, resorted to by devotees seeking relief from doshas connected with snakes. Sthanika Brahmins were its founding priests until the early 20th century, when the office passed to Shivalli Madhva Brahmins; worship now follows Madhvacharya's Tantrasara Sangraha.
story: The serpent king Vasuki is said to have hidden here from Garuda and to be worshipped alongside Kumaraswamy, who slew the demons Taraka and Shurapadmasura on the nearby Kumara Parvatha.

name: Kateel Durgaparameshwari Temple
significance: A Shakta temple standing on an islet in the middle of the Nandini river about 20 km from Mangalore, and one of the busiest temple towns of Tulu Nadu. Its founding date is not documented.

name: Mangaladevi Temple
significance: The temple at Bolar from which the city of Mangalore takes its name, built in the 9th century under the Alupa king Kundavarman with the encouragement of the Nath teacher Matsyendranath. It has a two-storeyed gateway tower in the Kerala manner and keeps a standing link with the Kadri Yogirajmutt, whose ascetics attend its festivals.
story: A Malabar princess named Parimala is said to have renounced her kingdom for Matsyendranath, who initiated her into the Nath order and renamed her Mangaladevi.

name: Chamundeshwari Temple
significance: The hilltop shrine of the tutelary goddess of the Mysore royal house, its original structure Hoysala work of the 12th century and its tower added under the Vijayanagara rulers. A stairway of a thousand steps was cut in 1659, and in 1664 Dodda Devaraja Wodeyar set a monolithic granite Nandi on the 700th step; the temple is counted among the eighteen Shakta pithas as Krauncha Pitha.
story: Durga is said to have killed the buffalo-demon Mahishasura on this hill, from which the town took the name Mahishuru, now Mysuru.

name: Srikanteshwara Temple, Nanjangud
significance: A large Shiva temple on the Kapila river whose origins go back to the Gangas, with the sanctum built in the Chola period around the 11th century and the front mandapa added under the Hoysalas. The seven-storey gopura, 120 feet high, was raised in 1845 by Devarajammanni, queen of Krishnaraja Wadiyar III; the 50,000 square foot complex holds 122 images of Shiva, 65 lingas and a stone Nandi installed in 1644.
story: Tipu Sultan's elephant is said to have recovered its sight after being bathed in the temple's sacred water for forty-eight days.

name: Biligiri Ranganatha Swamy Temple
significance: A hilltop shrine to Vishnu that gives the Biligiri Rangana Hills their name, set within a wildlife sanctuary declared in 1974 and made a tiger reserve in 2011. Its April festival draws pilgrims from across the region, and every second year the Soliga community presents the deity a hide slipper about one foot nine inches long.

name: Ghati Subramanya
significance: A temple about 60 km from Bengaluru, unusual in housing Subramanya and Narasimha together in one sanctum, and developed by the Ghorpade rulers of Sandur. It is one of the principal south Indian centres for the propitiation of Ketu.
story: Both images are believed to have risen out of the earth of their own accord, and childless couples who make vows here are held to be granted children.

name: Banashankari Amma Temple
significance: A goddess temple in Bagalkot district first raised under the Badami Chalukyas, with epigraphic evidence pointing to about 603 CE in the reign of Jagadekamalla I, whose house took the goddess as its tutelary deity. After the old Dravidian structure decayed, the Maratha chieftain Parusharam Agale rebuilt it in Vijayanagara style in 1750.
story: The Skanda and Padma Puranas tell of the goddess Shakambhari rising from the sacrificial fire to kill the demon Durgamasura, and of her feeding the country with vegetables during a famine, which gave her that name.

name: Mahakuta group of temples
significance: A Shaiva monastic complex of early Chalukya shrines gathered round the spring-fed Vishnu Pushkarni tank near Badami. The Mahakuta pillar inscription of 595-602 CE records a queen's grant of ten villages, Pattadakal and Aihole among them, and a later inscription of Vinapoti, a consort of King Vijayaditya, records gifts of rubies and silver; the shrines mix dravida tiered towers with nagara curvilinear ones in an early experiment towards vesara.

name: Lad Khan Temple
significance: One of the oldest surviving Hindu temples in India, at Aihole in Bagalkot district, now dated to about the 5th century rather than the 7th-8th as once thought. Its shrine, pillared mandapa of twelve carved columns, lattice windows and circumambulatory path translate timber building forms into stone; it was rededicated from Vishnu to Shiva, and takes its popular name from a man called Lad Khan who once lodged in it.

name: Bhoga Nandeeshwara Temple
significance: A twin-shrine complex at the foot of Nandi Hills, the northern Bhoganandishwara being the older and the Arunachaleswara added soon after, and described as the oldest surviving temple in the Nolambavadi manner of Dravidian architecture. Ganga, Hoysala and Vijayanagara rulers each added to it, and it is now a nationally protected monument under the Archaeological Survey of India.

name: Kotilingeshwara
significance: A modern temple founded in 1980 by Swami Sambha Shiva Murthy at Kammasandra in Kolar district, whose 15 acres hold a main Shivalinga 108 feet high, an 11-metre Nandi and roughly 650,000 smaller lingas donated by devotees and inscribed with their names. Eleven subsidiary shrines and pilgrim facilities stand on the site, which fills with visitors at Maha Shivaratri.
story: The first lingas are said to have been set up by a former atheist who became a devotee of Shiva, a story retold in the 2001 film Sri Manjunatha.

name: ISKCON Temple Bangalore
significance: One of the largest Krishna temples in the world, opened in May 1997 by President Shankar Dayal Sharma, with a gold-plated dhwaja-stambha 17 m high and a gilded kalasha shikhara of 8.5 m. Besides daily worship and free prasadam it runs the Akshaya Patra Foundation, which provides school meals across India.

name: Bull Temple (Dodda Basavana Gudi)
significance: Commissioned in 1537 by Kempe Gowda, the founder of Bengaluru, under Vijayanagara rule, this shrine holds one of the largest Nandi images anywhere, a granite monolith about 15 feet high and 20 feet long, blackened by generations of charcoal and oil. Its tower was added in the early 20th century, and the temple hosts the Kadalekaayi Parishe groundnut fair each Karthika month.

name: Gavi Gangadhareshwara Temple
significance: A monolithic cave temple in Bengaluru substantially renovated in the 16th century by Kempe Gowda I after his release from five years' imprisonment by Rama Raya. Its forecourt carries four monolithic pillars representing the damaru, trishula and two great discs, and each Makar Sankranti the setting sun passes between the horns of the Nandi outside to light the linga within the cave.
story: A tunnel inside the temple is said to lead all the way to Kashi.

name: Lakshmi Narasimha Temple, Nuggehalli
deity: Lakshmi Narasimha, with Keshava and Venugopala
significance: A trikuta Vaishnava temple in soapstone built in 1246 by the commander Bommanna Dandanayaka during the reign of the Hoysala king Vira Someshwara, in a town then called Vijaya Somanathapura and endowed as an agrahara. Its walls carry about 120 sculpted panels of deities and epic scenes, work attributed to the Hoysala sculptors Baichoja and Mallitamma.
